docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
• SNEPPX grad is reverse-mode (VJP tape) like jax.grad, but operates on Tensor objects rather than pytrees of ndarrays.
  • vmap is a thin NumPy-broadcasting shim — for production throughput, use the C/CUDA kernels (enable with SNEPPX_BUILD_CUDA=ON).
  • PyTree registration is not supported; pass flat Tensor lists to grad/jit.
  • Without the C backend, grad/jit fall back to a slow NumPy interpreter (functional, but not optimized) and Trainer.fit raises RuntimeError: C backend not available.

docs.title: Migrating from PyTorch to SNEPPX-Algo
docs.text: A side-by-side mapping from common torch APIs to SneppX_ALG equivalents. The SNEPPX Python layer mirrors PyTorch's ergonomics but requires the C backend (_HAS_C_BACKEND is True) for training; pure-NumPy fallbacks exist for inference-grade ops.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
# PyTorch
pip install torch
# SneppX
pip install sneppx-alg            # wheels include the C backend
# or from source:
git clone https://github.com/SneppX/sneppx-alg
cmake -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build --config Release

Set the path (from source builds):

$env:PYTHONPATH = "bindings/python"

docs.title: Tensor
docs.text:
PyTorch SNEPPX-Algo torch.tensor([...]) Tensor([...]) torch.zeros(4, 8) Tensor.zeros(4, 8) torch.randn(4, 8) Tensor.randn(4, 8) x.numpy() x.numpy() x.to("cuda") x.to("cuda") x @ y / x.matmul(y) x @ y (__matmul__) x.requires_grad x.requires_grad x.grad x.grad 
# PyTorch
import torch
x = torch.randn(4, 8)
w = torch.randn(8, 16, requires_grad=True)
y = x @ w
y.sum().backward()

# SNEPPX
from SneppX_ALG import Tensor
x = Tensor.randn((4, 8))
w = Tensor.randn((8, 16), requires_grad=True)
y = x @ w
y.backward()           # autodiff tape; requires C backend

Optimizers
docs.text:
PyTorch SNEPPX-Algo torch.optim.SGD SGD torch.optim.AdamW AdamW (Lion) Lion (LAMB) LAMB torch.optim.lr_scheduler.CosineAnnealingLR CosineAnnealingLR 
# PyTorch
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=2e-4, weight_decay=0.01)
sched = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.CosineAnnealingLR(opt, T_max=100)

# SNEPPX
from SneppX_ALG import AdamW, CosineAnnealingLR
opt   = AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=2e-4, weight_decay=0.01)
sched = CosineAnnealingLR(opt, min_lr=1e-5, max_lr=2e-4, total_steps=100)

docs.title: Training loop
docs.text:
PyTorch SNEPPX-Algo loss.backward() loss.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.step() optimizer.zero_grad() optimizer.zero_grad() (Trainer) Trainer.fit(loader) 
# SNEPPX — tape-based autodiff via the C backend
from SneppX_ALG import Tensor, AdamW, MSELoss
opt = AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
loss_fn = MSELoss()
for x, y in loader:
    opt.zero_grad()
    pred = model(x)
    loss = loss_fn(pred, y)
    loss.backward()
    opt.step()

The SneppX_ALG.Trainer class wraps the C training loop (Trainer.fit); for low-level control use the optimizer directly as above.

docs.text:

docs.text:
TensorFlow SNEPPX-Algo model.compile(loss=..., optimizer=...) Trainer(model, TrainConfig) model.fit(dataset, epochs=...) Trainer.fit(loader, epochs=N) model.evaluate(...) Trainer.evaluate(x, y) tf.GradientTape loss.backward() (tape autodiff) tf.config.optimizer.set_jit(True) CUDA kernels auto-selected when _HAS_CUDA 
# Keras
import tensorflow as tf
inputs = tf.keras.Input(shape=(784,))
x = tf.keras.layers.Dense(256, activation="relu")(inputs)
x = tf.keras.layers.Dropout(0.2)(x)
outputs = tf.keras.layers.Dense(10)(x)
model = tf.keras.Model(inputs, outputs)
model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss=tf.keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True))
model.fit(ds, epochs=10)

# SNEPPX (Keras-style API)
from SneppX_ALG import Input, Dense, Dropout, Model, AdamW, CrossEntropyLoss, Trainer, TrainConfig
from SneppX_ALG import TensorDataset, DataLoader

inputs = Input(shape=(784,))
x      = Dense(256, activation="relu")(inputs)
x      = Dropout(0.2)(x)
outputs = Dense(10)(x)
model   = Model(inputs, outputs)

cfg = TrainConfig(); cfg.learning_rate = 1e-3
trainer = Trainer(model, cfg)
loader  = DataLoader(TensorDataset(x_train, y_train), batch_size=32, shuffle=True)
for epoch in range(10):
    trainer.fit(loader)

from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings.jit import jit, grad
from SneppX_ALG import Tensor

@jit
def loss_fn(params, x, y):        # XLA-style compile when C backend present
    ...

docs.title: Migration guide: v0.9.7.890 → v0.9.7.890e
docs.text: Applies to: Anyone consuming SNEPPX-Alg who builds/trains the HSS model.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text: v0.9.7.890e is a drop-in correctness patch. No API, ABI, or build-flag changes. Rebuild and you get a working HSS backward pass.

docs.title: What you must do
docs.text:
Nothing — just pull the tag and rebuild:

git fetch --tags
git checkout v0.9.7.890e
cmake -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DSNEPPX_BUILD_TESTS=ON
cmake --build build --config Release
cd build && ctest -C Release --output-on-failure

The integration test test_train_integration is the regression guard for this fix.

docs.title: What changed under the hood
docs.text: Area Before (v0.9.7.890) After (v0.9.7.890e) backward_layer_norm gain read cast tensor pointer to float* (garbage) read tensor->data buffer (correct) sqrt in autodiff implicitly declared, returned -256.0 #include <math.h> added, correct value HSS training loss increased / diverged decreases >90% over 10 steps Debug prints present in ops.c/tape.c/test removed

docs.title: Behavior changes you may notice
docs.text:
• Training now actually learns. If you previously saw HSS training loss increase or NaN/explode, that was the bug. After upgrading, loss should decrease monotonically (modulo LR/step-count choices).
  • Determinism. With a fixed seed and SNEPPX_OPTIMIZER_ADAM, results are reproducible run-to-run (verified 15/15 Release runs).
  • No output-format change. Saved weights, checkpoints, and log lines are unchanged except for the removal of the temporary debug prints.

docs.title: If you forked kernel/autodiff/ops.c
docs.text:
If you maintain a local patch to ops.c, port these two changes:

  1. In backward_layer_norm, change float* gd = (float*)c->gamma->data; → float* gd = c->gamma ? (float*)c->gamma->data->data : NULL; (same for bd/beta).
  2. Add #include <math.h> near the top of ops.c.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: v1.0.0 is the first stable release of SNEPPX-Algo. All APIs introduced in the 0.9.x cycle are now frozen. No breaking changes to existing functionality.

docs.text: All version manifests have been bumped from 0.9.7.890e to 1.0.0.

docs.title: Bugfixes
docs.text:
1. model_card_to_json hang fixed — The 3rd argument to json_escape_append in the tags loop was &buf_len instead of &buf_size, causing an infinite realloc loop when serializing cards with tags. If you called model_card_to_json on a card with tags, it would hang. Now fixed.

  2. weight_collection_add buffer overrun fixed — memcpy used t->data_size (the allocated size, which may be larger) instead of data_size (the actual data size to copy). If data_size < t->data_size, this could read past the source buffer. Now clamped to min(data_size, t->data_size).

  3. test_model_card.c crash fixed — Missing #include <stdlib.h> caused malloc/free to be assumed extern int (32-bit), truncating 64-bit pointers on x64 → access violation. Test now uses proper setters instead of raw strdup into struct fields.

  4. Qwen2Config/DeepSeekV2Config max_seq_len fixed — The max_seq_len field was declared both as a @dataclass field and a @property (read-only), causing AttributeError: property has no setter on construction. Removed the duplicate field; max_seq_len is now only a @property that returns self.max_position_embeddings.

docs.title: Release v0.9.7.890e — HSS backward-corruption fix
docs.text: Date: 2026-07-18 Tag: v0.9.7.890e Type: Patch release (fixes the HSS training backward pass)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: v0.9.7.890e is a correctness patch for the Hierarchical State Space (HSS) training path. It does not change the public API. Two bugs that made test_train_integration diverge (loss increase instead of decrease) are fixed.

docs.title: 1. Layer-norm gamma/beta gradient pointer dereference (kernel/autodiff/ops.c)
docs.text:
In backward_layer_norm, the gain/shift parameters were read as:

float* gd = (float*)c->gamma->data;   /* WRONG: c->gamma->data is a tensor */
float* bd = c->beta ? (float*)c->beta->data : NULL;

c->gamma is a SNEPPXVariable*; c->gamma->data is its SNEPPXTensor*. Casting the tensor pointer to float* read the tensor struct's bytes as floats, yielding garbage gains. The fix reads the actual float buffer:

float* gd = c->gamma ? (float*)c->gamma->data->data : NULL;
float* bd = c->beta  ? (float*)c->beta->data->data  : NULL;

Consequence before the fix: the layer-norm input gradient (gx) was scaled by garbage gains, producing huge gradients that propagated through the whole graph and exploded the Adam parameter updates for x_proj / x_proj_bias.

docs.title: 2. Missing <math.h> — sqrt implicitly declared (kernel/autodiff/ops.c)
docs.text:
ops.c did not include <math.h>, so sqrt was implicitly declared (MSVC assumes int sqrt()). The call returned a constant -256.0 for every input, so inv_std = 1.0 / sqrt(var + eps) was wrong (≈ -0.0039 instead of ≈ 14.8), corrupting the input gradient of every layer-norm in the graph.

Fix: added #include <math.h>.

docs.title: 3. Diagnostics removed
docs.text: All debug instrumentation added during diagnosis ([LN*], [MSE*], [CAT*], [TR*], [RGTS], [MSENG], [TP-*] prints, the g_dbg_* globals, and the _CRTDBG flags in the integration test) has been removed.

init_loss = 0.234858
final_loss = 0.015788   (ratio 0.067 — >93% reduction over 10 Adam steps)

docs.title: Release v1.5.0 — Trainable Everything, Higher-Order Autograd, and the Python Ecosystem
docs.text: Date: 2026-10-17 Tag: v1.5.0 Type: Minor — large feature & correctness release

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
v1.5.0 is the largest autograd and Python-ecosystem release since v1.0.0. Every nn.* module that consumes a tensor is now end-to-end differentiable, the autograd tape gained higher-order (double-backward) support across 40+ ops plus forward/reverse-mode helpers, a PyTorch-style functional namespace was added, sparse tensors landed, and fourteen new pure-NumPy Python packages (metrics, datasets, sampling, regularization, callbacks, linalg, signal, graph, stats, structured_output, rag, agents, observability, speculative) were shipped with dedicated test suites.

A recurring theme of this release was finding and fixing silent correctness bugs that made models untrainable while still producing numerically plausible forward passes. Many of those bugs were caught by adding finite-difference and exact-analytic gradient tests.

docs.title: 1. Full differentiability — every nn module now trains
docs.text:
Prior to this release a significant number of nn modules used raw NumPy forward paths and therefore produced no autograd graph — the model would "run" but never learn. Each was rewritten to route through an autograd_ops Function with an exact analytic adjoint:

  • Convolutions: Conv1d, Conv2d, Conv3d (windowed-einsum grad-kernel, scatter-add grad-input; stride / padding / dilation aware).
  • Transposed convolutions: ConvTranspose1d/2d/3d (exact adjoint of the scatter formulation).
  • Normalization: LayerNorm, RMSNorm, BatchNorm1d/2d/3d, GroupNorm, InstanceNorm1d/2d/3d.
  • Embeddings: Embedding, EmbeddingBag (sum / mean / max).
  • Pooling: MaxPool1d/2d/3d, AvgPool1d/2d/3d, AdaptiveAvgPool1d/2d/3d, AdaptiveMaxPool1d/2d/3d, MaxUnpool1d/2d/3d, generic Pooling1d/2d/3d.
  • Resampling: Upsample (nearest + generic N-D multilinear bilinear/trilinear with PyTorch align_corners semantics), PixelShuffle, PixelUnshuffle, ChannelShuffle.
  • Geometry / shape: Unfold, Fold, differentiable permute, Flatten.
  • Metrics / heads: Bilinear, CosineSimilarity, PairwiseDistance.
  • Activations: LeakyReLU, ELU, SELU, CELU, PReLU, RReLU, LogSigmoid, Softplus, Softsign, Hardswish, Hardtanh, Mish, Hardsigmoid, Hardshrink, Softshrink, Tanhshrink, Threshold, GLU (notably LogSigmoid had an incorrect derivative that finite-difference tests caught).
  • Padding: ConstantPad / ZeroPad / ReflectionPad / ReplicationPad (1d / 2d / 3d).
  • Dropout: CPU path rewritten as a constant-mask multiply so gradients flow.

A repo-wide probe now reports zero non-differentiable nn modules.

docs.title: 2. Higher-order autograd + forward/reverse-mode helpers
docs.text:
• Tensor.backward(create_graph=True) and grad(..., create_graph=True) build a replayable graph so gradients themselves carry gradients.
  • create_graph branches added for 40+ operations, including Add, Sub, Mul, Div, MatMul, Transpose, Sum, Mean, Relu, Sigmoid, Tanh, Sqrt, Exp, Log, Pow, Reshape, GetItem, Linear, Gelu, Silu, Softmax, LogSoftmax, LayerNorm, RMSNorm, Abs, Squeeze, Unsqueeze, Dropout, Cat, Stack, Neg, Conv1d, and the loss functions (MSELoss, CrossEntropyLoss, KLDivLoss, NLLLoss, BCELoss, BCEWithLogitsLoss, SmoothL1Loss, HuberLoss).
  • Verified with exact Hessian reference tests (e.g. KLDiv 2·t·tᵀ/n², CrossEntropy 2·c·cᵀ, BCEWithLogits (1/N)·xᵀ·diag(s(1−s))·x, SmoothL1/Huber H = 2·dS·dSᵀ + 2·S·diag(d²S)).
  • Added jvp (forward-mode: J @ tangent) and vjp (reverse-mode) helpers in autograd.

docs.title: 3. Functional namespace — F.*
docs.text:
A PyTorch-mirroring functional API (sneppx_ALG.nn.functional, exported as F) with ~70 differentiable ops: activations, linear / conv1d/2d/3d / conv_transpose2d, pooling (incl. adaptive), layer / rms / batch / group / instance norm, padding, flatten / unflatten, unfold / fold, embedding / embedding_bag, 14 losses, interpolate, pixel_shuffle / channel_shuffle, one_hot, pad_sequence.

sx.functional remains reserved for the pre-existing autograd functional module (JVP/VJP) — use the F alias.

docs.title: 4. Sparse tensors
docs.text:
New sparse.py with a canonical COO storage type (SparseTensor), CSR / CSC / BSR layout constants and factories, dense interop, and ops:

  • sparse_mm (sparse@dense, sparse@sparse, dense@dense)
  • sparse_addmm, sparse_sum, sparse_softmax, sparse_conv2d
  • Tensor.to_sparse() / to_dense() and to_sparse_coo/csr/csc/bsr
  • optim.SparseAdam performs a real sparse step: moment buffers are read/written only at the grad's nonzero indices.

All pure-NumPy / stdlib, each with its own test suite:

Package Highlights metrics classification / regression / ranking metrics datasets synthetic + tabular dataset utilities sampling random / weighted / stratified samplers regularization weight decay, label smoothing, dropout helpers callbacks early stopping, LR schedulers, checkpoints linalg decompositions, solvers, norms signal windows, FFT helpers, filters graph adjacency structures, traversal, embedding helpers stats descriptive, distributions, scipy-free inference (t/χ² CIs, bootstrap, permutation) structured_output JSON-Schema subset validator, fence stripping, logit masking rag tokenization, chunking, BM25, hashing embeddings, hybrid retriever agents messages, tool registry, ReAct parsing, conversation memory, agent loop observability tracing/spans, timers, event bus, structured logging, metric registry speculative n-gram / prompt-lookup drafters, speculative verification & decoding

docs.title: 6. Optimizers
docs.text: Added Adam, NAdam, Rprop, ASGD, LBFGS, and SparseAdam (sparse-aware) alongside the existing SGD-family, plus full param_groups support.

docs.title: 7. Correctness & bug fixes
docs.text:
• Scalar-first autograd: 0.5 * x, 1.0 - x, 1.0 + x, 2.0 / x returned requires_grad=True but produced no gradient. Function.apply now records Tensor positions and realigns grads positionally.
  • Batched convolution (N>1): conv1d/2d/3d scrambled outputs for batch sizes > 1 (a bogus reshape/transpose that was only correct at N=1).
  • Conv args: Conv1d now adds bias with correct broadcasting.
  • Cat.backward used np.split(grad, sizes) (wrong — treats sizes as indices); fixed to np.cumsum(sizes)[:-1].
  • RMSNorm.backward used the normalized input where the raw input was required (spurious 1/rms factor).
  • Mul.backward leaked a raw ndarray into Tensor.* (re-entering forward).
  • Div.forward crashed on a scalar numerator; Pow.forward produced a shape-(0,) gradient when the exponent was a constant Tensor.
  • MatMul double-backward for 1-D vectors (xᵀw) via Unsqueeze/Squeeze.
  • MultiMarginLoss had a flipped margin sign (margin − x_j + x_y instead of margin − x_y + x_j).
  • load_state_dict(strict=True) now raises on missing/unexpected keys and reports size mismatches; register_buffer(persistent=False) excludes buffers from state_dict.

docs.title: S2 Obfuscation Layer Security Audit
docs.text: Date: 2026-08-16 Scope: security/obfuscation/obfuscation_advanced.cpp, obfuscation_advanced.h Classification: S2 — Obfuscation (Code transformation, string encryption, anti-debug) Auditor: Automated review of S2 layer

docs.title: Summary of Findings
docs.text: Severity Count Description Critical 3 Insecure RNG for obfuscation decisions, buffer overflow in junk code insertion, type-punning alignment High 2 Non-constant-time memory access in whitebox AES, IAT protection race condition Medium 2 Bogus CF trampoline overwrites real code unconditionally, array index obfuscation is reversible Low 1 Dead code in array obfuscation stride multiplication

docs.title: 1. SNEPPX_junk_code_insert (lines 130-141) — CWE-787 Buffer Overflow
docs.text:
size_t junk_len=0;
for (int i=0;i<16;i++) if (jcg->junk_code[idx][i]) junk_len=i+1;

CWE-787 (Out-of-bounds Write): The junk_code storage is uint8_t junk_code[64][16] (from header). The loop finds junk_len by scanning for non-zero bytes — but does not stop at SNEPPX_FAKE_BLOCK_SIZE boundary. If junk_code[idx] contains all 16 bytes non-zero, junk_len=16. Then:

if (*code_len+junk_len>max_len) return -1;

This correctly checks against max_len. However, memcpy(code+pos, jcg->junk_code[idx], junk_len) at line 138 writes junk_len bytes starting at pos. If pos + junk_len > *code_len + junk_len (i.e., pos > *code_len), this writes beyond the original code buffer. The position parameter (line 130: int position) is cast to int pos at line 136 with bounds checking, so this specific path is safe only if position >= 0. If position < 0, it defaults to code_len — OK. But the memmove at line 137 code+pos+junk_len could overlap if pos+2*junk_len > code_len... actually this is fine for memmove.

Lower severity in practice — the bounds check at line 135 catches the actual overflow. Marking as Medium (CWE-787 near-miss).

docs.title: 2. Use of rand() for obfuscation decisions — CWE-338 Insecure RNG
docs.text:
SNEPPX_bogus_seed();  // line 217: srand(seed)
int idx=rand()%jcg->junk_count;  // line 132
size_t len=(size_t)(rand()%12+2);  // line 231
uint8_t v=(uint8_t)(rand()&0xFF);  // line 233
int fake_idx=rand()%SNEPPX_bogus_int.count;  // line 285

CWE-338 (Use of Cryptographically Weak PRNG): The entire S2 obfuscation layer uses rand() + srand() seeded with std::chrono::steady_clock. An attacker who can predict or brute-force the seed (1-second granularity via time(NULL) or ~1μs from steady_clock with ~2^32 range depending on implementation) can reproduce: - Which junk pattern is inserted (defeats anti-disassembly) - Which fake block is used for trampoline (defeats control flow obfuscation) - All pattern bytes for bogus CF blocks

This makes the obfuscation deterministic and reproducible, completely defeating the purpose of S2. The seed is only set once (guarded by seeded flag), so all rand() calls throughout execution share the same PRNG state — a single prediction leaks all future obfuscation choices.

Recommendation: Replace rand() with SNEPPX_S1_secure_random() or a dedicated ChaCha20 DRBG from the S0 crypto layer. Never use rand() in security-sensitive code.

docs.title: 3. SNEPPX_whitebox_aes_init (lines 355-367) — CWE-1041 Type-Punning / Alignment
docs.text:
wb->te0[i]=s<<24|s<<16|s<<8|s;  // line 362

CWE-1041 (Type-Punning Undefined Behavior): The code casts uint8_t in[16] and uint8_t out[16] to uint32_t* at lines 377, 379, etc. On architectures requiring aligned access (e.g., ARMv6, some RISC-V), unaligned uint32_t* reads/writes cause SIGBUS. On x86 it works by accident. Use memcpy or std::bit_cast instead.

docs.title: 4. SNEPPX_bogus_cf_redirect (lines 279-302) — CWE-717 Incorrect Code Transformation
docs.text:
bcf->real_entry=(uintptr_t)code;  // saved
memcpy(code,trampoline,copy_len);  // OVERWRITES real code start
for (size_t i=flen;i<code_len;i++) {
    code[i]^=(uint8_t)((i*0x5A)^(fake_idx+1));  // XOR-encrypts body
}

CWE-717 (Incorrect Code Transformation): The function saves real_entry pointer but immediately overwrites the start of the real code with a trampoline (jump to fake block → jump back). The XOR loop encrypts the rest of the code. However: 1. There is no corresponding "restore" function — the encrypted code (code[i] ^= ...) can only be decrypted if fake_idx is known, which is stored only in SNEPPX_bogus_int.count (a global). If bogus_int.count changes between encrypt and decrypt, the code is permanently corrupted. 2. flen (fake block length) ranges from 2-12 bytes. The trampoline overwrite is copy_len = min(tp, code_len) where tp includes the fake block + 5-byte JMP. If code_len < 5, the trampoline is truncated and the JMP is incomplete → corrupted executable code.

Recommendation: Store decryption metadata alongside the real_entry pointer. Add SNEPPX_bogus_cf_restore().

docs.title: 5. SNEPPX_whitebox_aes_encrypt (lines 374-381+) — CWE-208 Timing Side-Channel
docs.text:
for (int r=1;r<=10;r++) {
    for (int i=0;i<4;i++) tk[i]=s[i];

The whitebox AES implementation accesses te0, te1, te2, te3 tables indexed by secret-dependent data (the state S). Table lookups are inherently timing-variable on any system with a cache hierarchy. The implementation provides no cache-safe masking or constant-time guarantees.

This contradicts the S2 threat model which claims "constant-time" operation. While whitebox cryptography inherently leaks via side channels (that's the design tradeoff), the S0-S9 model documents S1 as "constant-time by default" and S2 as "obfuscation" — but the whitebox AES here doesn't document its side-channel exposure.

Recommendation: Document the timing-exposure contract. Add a note that SNEPPX_whitebox_aes_* is obfuscation-only and must not be used for genuine secrecy.

docs.title: 6. SNEPPX_iat_protect_scan (lines 328-335) — CWE-362 Race Condition
docs.text:
int hooked=0;
for (int i=0;i<iat->count;i++) {
    if (iat->entries[i].original!=iat->entries[i].current) hooked++;
}

CWE-362 (Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource): The IAT entries original and current are void* pointers compared with !=. If another thread concurrently modifies current (e.g., via hot-patching), the read is non-atomic and may observe a torn pointer on 64-bit systems (though pointer writes are typically atomic on x86-64). More importantly, the hook detection is not constant-time — an attacker can measure how many entries are hooked via timing, leaking whether a hook is installed.

Recommendation: Use SNEPPX_ct_equal for pointer comparisons or document the non-constant-time nature.

docs.title: 7. SNEPPX_array_obfuscate_indices (lines 187-197) — CWE-327 Reversible Obfuscation
docs.text:
obfuscated_indices[j]^=0xDEADBEEF;  // line 194

The "obfuscation" is XOR with a hardcoded constant (0xDEADBEEF). This is trivially reversible — an attacker who reverse-engineers the binary recovers all obfuscated indices immediately. The stride multiplication loop (lines 190-193) adds no entropy; it's a deterministic transformation.

Recommendation: Use a per-process PRNG state seeded from the S0 CSPRNG, not a hardcoded constant.

docs.title: 8. Dead code in SNEPPX_array_obfuscate_indices (lines 190-196) — CWE-563
docs.text:
for (int i=ndim-1;i>=0;i--) {
    for (int j=0;j<n_indices;j++) obfuscated_indices[j]=(obfuscated_indices[j]%dims[i])*stride;
    stride*=dims[i];
}

CWE-563 (Dead Store): obfuscated_indices[j] is computed at line 191 but then immediately overwritten at line 195 (obfuscated_indices[j]+=linearized[j]*dims[ndim-1-i]). The stride multiplication loop is dead computation — it does work that is immediately discarded by the next line's +=. Only the final XOR at line 194 has any effect on the output.

docs.title: S0-S9 Model Alignment
docs.text:
Layer Documented Implemented Gap S2 Code transformation, string encryption, anti-debug ✓ obfuscation_advanced.cpp (binary subst, junk code, opaque pred, CFG flatten, IAT protect, bogus CF, whitebox AES) String encryption is in separate string_encrypt.cpp — verify it's not using the same rand() S7 Secure updates, rollback protection security/updates/ N/A — outside S2 scope S8 Formal verification security/formal/ N/A — outside S2 scope S9 Pentest, self-audit security/pentest/ N/A — outside S2 scope

The S2 layer documentation in docs/security_layers.md correctly lists the implemented components. However, it does not document the known timing and RNG weaknesses identified above.

docs.title: Threat Modeling Overview
docs.text: This directory contains threat modeling artifacts for the SNEPPX-ALG platform.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
SNEPPX-ALG uses the following threat modeling methodologies:

  1. STRIDE (Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service, Elevation of Privilege)
  2. PASTA (Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis)
  3. Attack Trees - Hierarchical representation of attacker goals and sub-goals
  4. DREAD (Damage, Reproducibility, Exploitability, Affected Users, Discoverability)
  5. LINDUN (Linkability, Identifiability, Non-repudiation, Detectability, Disclosure of information, Unawareness, Non-compliance)

docs.title: Process
docs.text:
1. Define system scope and boundaries
  2. Identify assets and trust boundaries
  3. Enumerate threats (STRIDE per component)
  4. Rank threats (DREAD)
  5. Identify mitigations
  6. Validate with attack tree analysis
  7. Document residual risks

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
• HSS: Timing side-channels via state transition matrix access patterns
  • SER: Expert weight leakage via routing patterns
  • ARC: Adversarial robustness, gradient leakage, model inversion
  • NPE: Bytecode tampering, register side-channels, JIT poisoning
  • FM: Gradient inversion, differential privacy budget exhaustion
  • S0-S9: Full security layer threat analysis

docs.title: Artifacts
docs.text:
• attack_tree.h - C header defining attack tree data structures
  • stride_model_core.h - C header defining STRIDE model data structures
  • threat_modeling_overview.md - This document (methodology overview)
  • STRIDE per-component spreadsheets (in docs/)
  • Attack trees per-component (in docs/)
  • DREAD risk matrices (in docs/)

docs.title: Risk Rating (DREAD)
docs.text: Rating Range Response CRITICAL 9-10 Immediate fix required HIGH 7-8 Fix within 30 days MEDIUM 4-6 Fix within 90 days LOW 1-3 Accept or fix next release

docs.title: Tutorial — Image Classification with SNEPPX
docs.text: Notebook: classification.ipynb (download)

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text: A small MLP classifier trained on synthetic 8×8 image data, using the SNEPPX nn module and AdamW optimizer. You'll see how Tensor operator overloads, Linear, LayerNorm, and CrossEntropyLoss compose, and how to log loss with the built-in Profiler.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
$env:PYTHONPATH = "bindings/python"

import numpy as np
from SneppX_ALG import (
    Tensor, Module, Sequential, Linear, LayerNorm, GELU, Dropout,
    AdamW, CrossEntropyLoss, CosineAnnealingLR, Profiler, Timer,
)
HAS_C = __import__("SneppX_ALG")._HAS_C_BACKEND

docs.title: 1. Synthetic data
docs.text:
We use 8×8 "images" with 10 classes:

def make_data(n=640):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    X = rng.standard_normal((n, 64)).astype(np.float32)
    y = rng.integers(0, 10, size=(n,)).astype(np.int64)
    return Tensor.from_numpy(X), Tensor.from_numpy(y)

docs.title: 2. The model
docs.text:
class Classifier(Module):
    def __init__(self, in_dim=64, hidden=128, classes=10):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = Sequential(
            Linear(in_dim, hidden), GELU(),
            LayerNorm(hidden),
            Linear(hidden, hidden), GELU(),
            Dropout(0.1),
            Linear(hidden, classes),
        )
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.net(x)

model = Classifier()

docs.title: 3. Train (needs C backend for backward)
docs.text:
X, y = make_data()
opt  = AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=2e-3, weight_decay=1e-4)
sched = CosineAnnealingLR(opt, min_lr=1e-5, max_lr=2e-3, total_steps=200)
prof = Profiler(enabled=True)

for step in range(200):
    idx = np.random.randint(0, X.shape[0], 64)
    xb, yb = X[idx], y[idx]
    with Timer(prof, "forward"):
        logits = model(xb)
        loss = CrossEntropyLoss()(logits, yb)
    if not HAS_C:
        print("C backend not available — skipping backward/step")
        break
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step(); sched.step()
    if step % 25 == 0:
        print(step, loss.item())
prof.print_summary()

docs.title: 4. Evaluate
docs.text:
def accuracy(model, X, y, batch=128):
    if not HAS_C:
        return 0.0
    correct = 0
    for i in range(0, len(X), batch):
        preds = model(X[i:i+batch]).data.argmax(-1)
        correct += (preds == y[i:i+batch].data).sum()
    return correct / len(X)

print("accuracy:", accuracy(model, X, y))

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Tensor overloads +, @, * — write math, not matmul() calls.
  • Linear uses PyTorch layout (out, in) weight, i.e. x @ W.T + b.
  • CrossEntropyLoss expects logits of shape (N, C) and targets (N,).
  • Without the C backend, backward()/step() are unavailable — build the extension first (cmake --build build --config Release).

docs.text:

docs.title: Tutorial — Data Pipeline
docs.text: Notebook: data_pipeline.ipynb (download)

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text: A complete data pipeline: train a SimpleTokenizer on text, encode/decode, batch with DataLoader + DistributedSampler, and serve batches to a model.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
$env:PYTHONPATH = "bindings/python"

import numpy as np, os
from SneppX_ALG import SimpleTokenizer, Tokenizer, Tensor
from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings.data_loader import DataLoader, TensorDataset
HAS_C = __import__("SneppX_ALG")._HAS_C_BACKEND

docs.title: 1. SimpleTokenizer (no HF deps)
docs.text:
corpus = ["hello world sneppx", "hello neural engine", "sneppx is fast",
          "neural networks rock", "sneppx sneppx hello"]

tok = SimpleTokenizer(vocab_size=50)
tok.train(corpus, min_freq=1)
ids = tok.encode("hello sneppx")
print("ids:", ids)
print("text:", tok.decode(ids))

docs.title: 2. Production tokenizer (HF tokenizers JSON)
docs.text:
# If you have a tokenizer.json from HuggingFace:
if os.path.exists("tokenizer.json"):
    ptok = Tokenizer("tokenizer.json")
    print("vocab size:", ptok.vocab_size)
    print("bos/eos/pad:", ptok.bos_token_id, ptok.eos_token_id, ptok.pad_token_id)
    print(ptok.decode(ptok.encode("Hello, world!")))
else:
    print("no tokenizer.json present — using SimpleTokenizer")

docs.title: 3. Chat template formatting
docs.text:
ptok = Tokenizer(vocab_size=32000)     # falls back to SimpleTokenizer
messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You are SNEPPX, a helpful assistant."},
    {"role": "user",   "content": "Summarize neural programming engines."},
]
prompt = ptok.apply_chat_template(messages)
ids = ptok.encode(prompt)
print(prompt)

docs.title: 4. TensorDataset + DataLoader
docs.text:
X = np.random.randint(0, 300, (200, 16)).astype(np.int64)   # token ids
Y = np.random.randint(0, 300, (200, 16)).astype(np.int64)   # labels
ds = TensorDataset(Tensor.from_numpy(X), Tensor.from_numpy(Y))
loader = DataLoader(ds, batch_size=32, shuffle=True)

for xb, yb in loader:
    print("batch:", xb.shape, yb.shape)    # (32, 16) (32, 16)

docs.title: 5. Streaming large corpora (mmap)
docs.text:
from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings.data_loader import (
    MemoryMappedTextDataset, StreamingTokenDataset,
)

# Random-access over a huge file via mmap
mmap_ds = MemoryMappedTextDataset(path="big_corpus.txt", tokenizer=tok, seq_len=512)

# Streaming webdataset-style shard reader
stream = StreamingTokenDataset(path="data/shard_*.jsonl", tokenizer=tok, seq_len=1024)

docs.title: 6. Distributed sharding
docs.text:
from SneppX_ALG import DistributedSampler, get_world_size, get_rank

sampler = DistributedSampler(ds, num_replicas=get_world_size(), rank=get_rank(), shuffle=True)
loader  = DataLoader(ds, batch_size=32, sampler=sampler)
sampler.set_epoch(epoch)      # re-shuffle per epoch

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• SimpleTokenizer (word-level) needs no dependencies; Tokenizer wraps HF tokenizers for BPE/WordPiece when available.
  • Special tokens: <pad>=0, <unk>=1, <s>=2, </s>=3.
  • DataLoader lives in interface_bindings.data_loader — not re-exported via from SneppX_ALG import *.
  • apply_chat_template emits <|system|> / <|user|> / <|assistant|> tags.
  • CPU-safe throughout (no C backend needed for the data pipeline).

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Tokenize + generate text — see Text Generation.
  • Build a language-model dataset for distributed training — see Distributed Training.

docs.title: Tutorial — Distributed Training
docs.text: Notebook: distributed_training.ipynb (download)

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text: A single script that trains a model with DDP-style gradient sync and ZeRO-1 optimizer-state sharding, runnable as 1-process-per-GPU via SneppX_ALG.launch. The notebook also covers DistributedSampler and the FSDP (ZeRO-3) path.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
cmake -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build --config Release
$env:PYTHONPATH = "bindings/python"

import numpy as np
from SneppX_ALG import (
    Transformer, DistributedWrapper, AdamW, CrossEntropyLoss,
    DistributedSampler, get_world_size, get_rank,
    init_process_group, destroy_process_group, FullyShardedDataParallel,
    FSDPConfig, ShardingStrategy, launch, TensorDataset, Tensor,
)
from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings.data_loader import DataLoader
HAS_C = __import__("SneppX_ALG")._HAS_C_BACKEND

docs.title: 1. The training function (runs in each rank)
docs.text:
def main():
    init_process_group(backend="nccl")       # reads WORLD_SIZE/RANK env
    rank = get_rank(); world = get_world_size()
    print(f"rank {rank}/{world}")

    model = Transformer(vocab_size=800, dim=256, num_heads=4, num_layers=4, ffn_dim=1024, max_seq_len=64)
    dp_model = DistributedWrapper(model, device="cuda" if world > 1 else "cpu")

    # synthetic sharded data
    X = Tensor.randn((256, 64)); y = Tensor(np.random.randint(0, 800, (256, 64)))
    ds = TensorDataset(X, y)
    sampler = DistributedSampler(ds, num_replicas=world, rank=rank, shuffle=True)
    loader = DataLoader(ds, batch_size=32, sampler=sampler)

    opt = AdamW(dp_model.parameters(), lr=2e-4, weight_decay=0.01)
    for epoch in range(2):
        sampler.set_epoch(epoch)
        for xb, yb in loader:
            logits = dp_model(xb)
            loss = CrossEntropyLoss()(logits.reshape((-1, 800)), yb.reshape((-1,)))
            opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); dp_model.sync_gradients(); opt.step()
        if rank == 0:
            print(f"epoch {epoch} loss={loss.item():.4f}")
    destroy_process_group()

docs.title: 2. Launch 2 GPUs (or 2 processes)
docs.text:
if __name__ == "__main__":
    launch(main, num_nodes=1, num_gpus=2)

launch spawns torch.distributed.run under the hood when num_nodes * num_gpus > 1; otherwise it calls main() directly — so the notebook cell can be run as-is for a smoke test with WORLD_SIZE=1.

docs.title: 3. ZeRO-1 (shard optimizer state) with FSDP
docs.text:
For larger models, wrap in FullyShardedDataParallel (FULL_SHARD = ZeRO-3):

base = Transformer(vocab_size=800, dim=512, num_heads=8, num_layers=12, ffn_dim=2048, max_seq_len=128)
fsdp_cfg = FSDPConfig(
    sharding=ShardingStrategy.FULL_SHARD,
    mixed_precision=MixedPrecision(param="bf16", reduce="fp32"),
)
model = FullyShardedDataParallel(base, fsdp_cfg)
# model.parameters() are now sharded; grads all-reduce on backward (C backend)

docs.title: 4. ZeRO-2/3 directly (CPU/CUDA kernel)
docs.text:
/* kernel/distributed/zero.c */
SNEPPX_ZeROOptimizer* zopt = SNEPPX_zero_optimizer_create(
    opt, world_size, rank, /*stage=*/3);
SNEPPX_zero_step(zopt, grads, n_grads, params, n_params);

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• DistributedWrapper.sync_gradients() divides grads by world_size after the all-reduce — so use the local loss, not loss / world_size.
  • DistributedSampler.set_epoch() must be called each epoch to re-shuffle across ranks.
  • launch short-circuits for single-process runs — great for smoke tests.
  • FSDP FULL_SHARD is the recommended way to fit 7B+ models on 4× GPUs.
  • NCCL must be on PATH/LD_LIBRARY_PATH; without it the Python side falls back to no-op collectives (pass-throughs data).

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Combine with RLHF on LoRA adapters for PPO.
  • Use Profiling & Benchmarks to spot communication bubbles.

docs.title: Tutorial — RLHF Fine-Tuning with LoRA + DPO
docs.text: Notebook: fine_tuning_rlhf.ipynb (download)

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text: A parameter-efficient fine-tuning recipe that (1) attaches LoRA adapters to a small model, (2) trains with DPO (Direct Preference Optimization) via SneppX_ALG.DPOTrainer, and (3) exercises the S5 AI safety filter on the generated output.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
$env:PYTHONPATH = "bindings/python"

import numpy as np
from SneppX_ALG import (
    Transformer, Tokenizer, AdamW, Tensor,
    DPOTrainer, LoRAConfig, LoRALinear,
    S5RLHFSafety, S5OutputVerifier,
)
HAS_C = __import__("SneppX_ALG")._HAS_C_BACKEND

docs.title: 1. Attach LoRA adapters
docs.text:
LoRA freezes the base weights and injects low-rank A·B updates into attention projections.

base = Transformer(vocab_size=300, dim=128, num_heads=4, num_layers=4, ffn_dim=256, max_seq_len=64)

lora_cfg = LoRAConfig(r=8, alpha=32, dropout=0.1)
# Wrap a Linear in a LoRA-augmented layer
base.lm_head = LoRALinear(base.lm_head, r=lora_cfg.r, alpha=lora_cfg.alpha)
print("trainable params:", sum(p.numel for n, p in base.named_parameters() if "lora_" in n))

docs.title: 2. DPOTrainer
docs.text:
DPO optimizes the policy to prefer chosen over rejected completions.

trainer = DPOTrainer(
    policy=base,
    ref_policy=None,            # uses policy as its own reference on first call
    beta=0.1,
    optimizer=AdamW(filter(lambda p: p.requires_grad, base.parameters()), lr=5e-4),
)

# Toy preference data: (prompt, chosen_tail, rejected_tail) token-id lists
prefs = [
    ([1, 2, 3], [10, 11, 12], [99, 98]),
    ([4, 5, 6], [20, 21],    [88, 87, 86]),
]
for prompt, chosen, rejected in prefs:
    if not HAS_C:
        print("C backend required for DPO backward — skipping")
        break
    loss = trainer.dpo_loss(
        prompt_input_ids=prompt,
        chosen_input_ids=chosen,
        rejected_input_ids=rejected,
    )
    trainer.optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    trainer.optimizer.step()
    print("dpo loss:", float(loss.data))

The DPO loss is loss = -log_σ(β·(logπ(y_w|x) − logπ(y_l|x) − (β/r)·logπ_ref/ratio)). DPOTrainer._forward_logps computes log-probs with proper softmax.

docs.title: 3. GRPO alternative
docs.text:
from SneppX_ALG import GRPOTrainer

grpo = GRPOTrainer(
    policy=base,
    optimizer=AdamW(base.parameters(), lr=3e-4),
    num_generations=4,
    beta=0.01,
)
# grpo_loss = ratio-based PPO surrogate; see trainer_v3

docs.title: 4. Safety-check the output
docs.text:
Run the generated continuation through the S5 safety layers:

prompt = "Explain how to..."
verifier = S5OutputVerifier()
safe = S5RLHFSafety(allowed_topics=["science", "technology"])
# After generation, verify + filter:
#   verifier.check(output_text)   -> bool
#   safe.is_safe(output_text)     -> bool

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• LoRA keeps the full model frozen and trains only injected low-rank weights — cheap to checkpoint/export.
  • DPO needs backward() (C backend). GRPO is the PPO-style alternative.
  • Always run S5OutputVerifier / S5RLHFSafety before serving RLHF-tuned output (S5 layer).
  • Checkpoints are small (only adapter weights); merge via apply_lora.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Quantize the fine-tuned model — see Quantization + Serving.
  • Serve with sneppx-serve --rlhf-safety to apply S5 filters at the API.

docs.title: Tutorial — Text Generation
docs.text: Notebook: generation.ipynb (download)

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text: A minimal causal-LM generation loop using the SNEPPX Transformer and the sampling/beam-search utilities in SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings.generation.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
$env:PYTHONPATH = "bindings/python"

import numpy as np
from SneppX_ALG import Transformer, Tokenizer, Tensor
from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings.generation import (
    generate, GenerationConfig, TextStreamer, TokenStreamer,
)
HAS_C = __import__("SneppX_ALG")._HAS_C_BACKEND

docs.title: 1. A tiny model
docs.text:
We keep vocab/size small so the NumPy path is fast enough to preview behavior.

model = Transformer(
    vocab_size=200, dim=64, num_heads=4, num_layers=2,
    ffn_dim=128, max_seq_len=64, dropout=0.0,
)
model.eval()

docs.title: 2. Greedy search (do_sample=False)
docs.text:
cfg = GenerationConfig(max_new_tokens=24, do_sample=False)
ids = [1, 2, 3]                       # BOS, token, token
out = generate(model, ids, generation_config=cfg)
print(out["output_ids"])              # (1, 3 + 24)

docs.title: 3. Sampling with top-k + top-p
docs.text:
cfg = GenerationConfig(
    max_new_tokens=48,
    do_sample=True,
    temperature=0.8,
    top_k=40,
    top_p=0.9,
    repetition_penalty=1.15,
)
out = generate(model, ids, generation_config=cfg)
print("final length:", out["output_ids"].shape)

generate picks the strategy automatically:

Condition Strategy num_beams > 1 beam search do_sample and temperature > 1e-6 sampling (top-k/top-p) otherwise greedy

docs.title: 4. Beam search
docs.text:
cfg = GenerationConfig(
    max_new_tokens=32,
    num_beams=3,
    length_penalty=0.7,
    early_stopping=True,
)
out = generate(model, ids, generation_config=cfg)

docs.title: 5. Stream tokens live
docs.text:
tok = Tokenizer(vocab_size=200)
stream = TextStreamer(tokenizer=tok, skip_prompt=True)
out = generate(model, ids, generation_config=GenerationConfig(max_new_tokens=40), streamer=stream)
# tokens print as they are produced

For raw IDs instead of text, swap TextStreamer for TokenStreamer and read stream.get_tokens().

docs.title: 6. Batch generation (variable-length prompts)
docs.text:
from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings.generation import batch_generate

prompts = [[1,2,3], [1,4,5,6,7], [1,8,9]]
cfg = GenerationConfig(max_new_tokens=16, temperature=0.7)
out = batch_generate(model, prompts, generation_config=cfg)
print(out["output_ids"].shape)       # (3, max_len + 16)

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• generate expects a model whose forward(input_ids=..., past_key_values=..., use_cache=True) returns {"logits", "past_key_values"}; Transformer returns logits directly, so wrap it for true KV-cache decoding in production (see docs/API.md).
  • CPU-safe NumPy sampling loop works without the C backend — just slower.
  • repetition_penalty, top_k, top_p, and stop_strings are all configurable via GenerationConfig (or **kwargs override).

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Pair with a real Tokenizer (HF tokenizers JSON) — see Data Pipeline.
  • Serve the model with sneppx-serve — see Quantization + Serving.

docs.title: Tutorial — Model Conversion (HF → SNEPPX)
docs.text: Notebook: model_conversion.ipynb (download)

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text: Convert a HuggingFace-style model directory (.safetensors + config.json) into a SNEPPX checkpoint (.sneppx) using convert_hf_to_sneppx, inspect the weight-name remapping, and load it back with CheckpointReader.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
$env:PYTHONPATH = "bindings/python"
# You need an HF model dir on disk (safetensors + config.json).
# Example: download via `huggingface-cli download` or use a local copy.

import os, json, glob
from SneppX_ALG import (
    from_pretrained, get_model_config, list_available_models,
    read_safetensors, convert_hf_to_sneppx, HF_WEIGHT_MAP,
)
from SneppX_ALG import CheckpointReader, validate_checkpoint
HAS_C = __import__("SneppX_ALG")._HAS_C_BACKEND

docs.title: 1. Pick a supported family
docs.text:
print(list_available_models())     # ['llama2:7B', 'llama2:13B', 'llama3:8B', 'mistral:7B', 'qwen2:7B', ...]

cfg = get_model_config("mistral", "7B")   # config + param estimate
print(cfg["hidden_size"], cfg["num_hidden_layers"], cfg["num_attention_heads"])

docs.title: 2. Inspect the weight name map
docs.text:
print("HF -> SneppX name remaps (non-layer):")
for hf_name, sx_name in HF_WEIGHT_MAP["mistral"].items():
    print(f"  {hf_name:40s} -> {sx_name}")

Layer weights follow the pattern:

model.layers.{i}.{submodule}.weight   ->   layers.{i}.{remapped}.weight
model.embed_tokens.weight            ->   embedding.weight
model.norm.weight                    ->   norm.weight
lm_head.weight                       ->   lm_head.weight

docs.title: 3. Read a safetensors file directly
docs.text:
meta, tensors = read_safetensors("models/mistral-7b/model.safetensors")
print("metadata:", meta)
print("tensors found:", len(tensors))
sample = next(iter(tensors))
print(sample, "bytes:", len(tensors[sample]))

docs.title: 4. Convert to a .sneppx checkpoint
docs.text:
n = convert_hf_to_sneppx(
    hf_dir="models/mistral-7b",
    family="mistral",
    output_path="/ckpts/mistral-7b.sneppx",
    verbose=True,
)
print(f"converted {n} weights")

convert_hf_to_sneppx writes via CheckpointWriter (binary format with header + tensor records + metadata), so the result is S7-signed-update ready. Missing weights are written as zero-byte placeholders and logged as WARNING.

docs.title: 5. Validate + read back
docs.text:
ok, errs = validate_checkpoint("/ckpts/mistral-7b.sneppx")
print("valid:", ok, "errors:", errs)

reader = CheckpointReader("/ckpts/mistral-7b.sneppx")
meta_out = reader.metadata()
print(meta_out["family"], meta_out["num_converted"])

# Read a specific tensor (returns numpy)
w = reader.read_tensor("layers.0.attn.q_proj.weight")
print(w.shape, w.dtype)

docs.title: 6. From a config dict → nn.Transformer
docs.text:
from SneppX_ALG import build_transformer_from_config

cfg = get_model_config("llama2", "7B")
model = build_transformer_from_config(cfg)    # nn.Module (NumPy path)
print("params:", sum(p.numel for p in model.parameters()))

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• convert_hf_to_sneppx is the only supported path for real weights. from_pretrained returns a config dict, not weights.
  • HF_WEIGHT_MAP covers llama2, llama3, mistral, qwen2, deepseek_v2 (LLaMA-3 reuses LLaMA-2 mappings).
  • read_safetensors is a standalone TLV parser — no safetensors package required.
  • .sneppx checkpoints are S7-signed-update ready; verify with sneppx-analyze verify before serving.
  • CPU-safe (conversion is NumPy); loading weights into Transformer.forward for generation needs the C backend.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Quantize the converted checkpoint — see Quantization & Serving.
  • Inspect with the CheckpointReader in Checkpointing.

docs.title: Tutorial — MoE SER Expert Routing
docs.text: Notebook: moe_ser_routing.ipynb (download)

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text: A sparse Mixture-of-Experts layer using SNEPPX's SER module: route each token to the top-2 of 8 experts, compute the load-balancing loss, and inspect the routing distribution to detect expert collapse.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
$env:PYTHONPATH = "bindings/python"

import numpy as np
from SneppX_ALG import SERModel, SERConfig, Tensor
HAS_C = __import__("SneppX_ALG")._HAS_C_BACKEND

docs.title: 1. Configure an 8-expert, top-2 MoE
docs.text:
cfg = SERConfig()
cfg.num_experts = 8
cfg.num_active  = 2        # top-k
cfg.input_dim   = 64
cfg.expert_dim  = 128
cfg.output_dim  = 64
cfg.top_k_method = 0       # softmax routing
cfg.load_balance_coef = 0.01
cfg.dropout_rate = 0.0

moe = SERModel(cfg, seed=42, num_layers=1)

docs.title: 2. Forward pass
docs.text:
x = Tensor.randn((4, 16, cfg.input_dim))   # (batch, seq, dim)
out = moe.forward(x)                         # (4, 16, 64)

docs.title: 3. Inspect routing weights
docs.text:
With the C backend, the router probabilities are exposed via the SNEPPXSERRouter; here we approximate the load-balancing signal with a pure-NumPy router replica:

if not HAS_C:
    # Pure-NumPy illustration of the top-k routing math
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    router_logits = rng.standard_normal((16, 8))      # (seq, num_experts)
    scores = np.softmax(router_logits, axis=-1)
    top2 = np.argsort(-scores, axis=-1)[:, :2]
    load = np.zeros(8)
    for t in range(16):
        load[top2[t]] += 1
    print("tokens-per-expert:", load.astype(int))

docs.title: 4. Load-balancing loss
docs.text:
# C backend: moe.load_balance_loss(routing_weights)
# Pure-Python approximation:
routes = np.zeros(8)
for t in range(16):
    routes[top2[t]] += 1
frac = routes / 16.0
p_avg = scores.mean(axis=0)
loss = float(np.sum(frac * p_avg) * cfg.load_balance_coef)
print("balance loss:", loss)      # lower + uniform is better

docs.title: 5. Stacked MoE layers
docs.text:
class MoETransformer(Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.inp = Linear(64, 64)
        self.moe = SERModel(SERConfig(), seed=1, num_layers=4)   # 4 stacked MoE layers
        self.out = Linear(64, 64)
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.out(self.moe.forward(self.inp(x)))

net = MoETransformer()

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• num_active (top-k) must be ≤ num_experts; increasing k raises FLOPs linearly but improves quality.
  • load_balance_coef trades quality for uniform expert usage; 0.01 is the default in the C config.
  • Expert parallelism (EP) shards experts across GPUs — set ep_size = num_experts / tp_size in DistributedConfig.
  • Without the C backend (_HAS_C_BACKEND is False), SERModel.forward raises RuntimeError: C backend not available — the illustration above shows the equivalent NumPy math.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Combine with Distributed Training for EP across nodes (see algorithms/ser/core/gater.c all-to-all dispatch).
  • Add a learned MLP gater (use_mlp_gater=1 in SNEPPXSERConfig).

docs.title: Tutorial — Profiling & Benchmarks
docs.text: Notebook: profiling_benchmarks.ipynb (download)

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text: Instrument a forward+backward pass with the Profiler/Timer, track peak memory with MemoryTracker, and run a regression benchmark with the sneppx-bench CLI.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
$env:PYTHONPATH = "bindings/python"

import numpy as np, time
from SneppX_ALG import (
    Transformer, Linear, GELU, Tensor, AdamW,
    Profiler, Timer, MemoryTracker, get_profiler, timeit,
)
HAS_C = __import__("SneppX_ALG")._HAS_C_BACKEND

docs.title: 1. Profile a region
docs.text:
model = Transformer(vocab_size=500, dim=256, num_heads=4, num_layers=4, ffn_dim=1024, max_seq_len=64)
x = Tensor.randn((8, 64))

prof = Profiler(enabled=True)
with Timer(prof, "forward"):
    out = model(x)
with Timer(prof, "loss"):
    loss = out.data.mean()      # pure-NumPy surrogate (no C backend needed)
prof.print_summary()

docs.title: 2. Global profiler + @timeit
docs.text:
g = get_profiler(); g.enabled = True
g.reset()

@timeit(g)
def step(x):
    return model(x)

for _ in range(5):
    step(x)
print(g.to_json())             # structured JSON for dashboards

docs.title: 3. Memory tracking
docs.text:
mt = MemoryTracker()
mt.start()
for _ in range(10):
    _ = model(x)
peak = mt.peak(); mt.checkpoint("after-10")
mt.stop()
print("peak bytes:", peak)

docs.title: 4. Benchmark with sneppx-bench (regression)
docs.text:
sneppx-bench run tests/python/test_tensor.py \
    --repeat 10 --save results/bench_$(git rev-parse --short HEAD).json
# Compare two runs:
sneppx-bench compare results/bench_a.json results/bench_b.json

Flags: --repeat N, --warmup N, --filter <regex>, --save PATH, --unit <ms|s|us>. The tool tracks regressions against a local history under ~/.sneppx/.

docs.title: 5. CPU timing (no C backend) — fallback
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from SneppX_ALG import Tensor

# When the C backend is absent we still get deterministic shapes; just time it.
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for _ in range(20):
    y = model(x)
dt = (time.perf_counter() - t0) / 20
print(f"fwd {dt*1000:.2f} ms")

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Profiler aggregates by named region; Timer is the context-manager form.
  • get_profiler() returns the global profiler reused by @timeit.
  • On CUDA, NVTX markers (SNEPPX_USE_NVTX) are emitted automatically — import into nsys / nvtx UIs.
  • sneppx-bench stores results tagged with the git SHA for regression diffs.
  • The C core also ships kernel/profiler.c (SNEPPX_Profiler) for C-side instrumentation; the Python Profiler is its mirror.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Profile the quantized model — see Quantization & Serving.
  • Read docs/PROGRESS_TENSOR.md and docs/BENCHMARKS.md for full perf tables.

docs.title: Tutorial — Quantization & Serving
docs.text: Notebook: quantization_serving.ipynb (download)

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text: Quantize the weights of a small Transformer to INT4 (AWQ) and FP8, measure the error/SNR, estimate the on-disk size, and launch the sneppx-serve FastAPI server with an authenticated, quantized model.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
$env:PYTHONPATH = "bindings/python"
# Serving deps (optional):
python -m pip install "sneppx-alg[serve]"

import numpy as np
from SneppX_ALG import (
    Transformer, Tensor, AdamW,
    QuantMode, quantize_int8_sym, dequantize_int8_sym,
    quantize_int4_sym, dequantize_int4_sym,
    quantize_int8_channel, dequantize_int8_channel,
    awq_quantize, awq_scale_weights, quantize_error,
)
from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings.quantized_serve import (
    QuantizedModelConfig, quantize_model_weights,
    dequantize_weights, estimate_model_size_mb,
)
HAS_C = __import__("SneppX_ALG")._HAS_C_BACKEND

docs.title: 1. A small model + its raw weights
docs.text:
model = Transformer(vocab_size=500, dim=128, num_heads=4, num_layers=2, ffn_dim=256, max_seq_len=64)
params = {name: p.data.copy() for name, p in model.named_parameters()}
print("FP32 size MB:", sum(v.nbytes for v in params.values()) / 1e6)

docs.title: 2. Per-tensor INT8 sanity check
docs.text:
w = Tensor.from_numpy(params["lm_head.weight"].astype(np.float32))
qw, scale = quantize_int8_sym(w)
wq = dequantize_int8_sym(qw, scale)
print("INT8 SNR (dB):", quantize_error(w, wq, metric="snr"))

docs.title: 3. Per-channel INT8 (lower error)
docs.text:
qw, scales = quantize_int8_channel(w, dim=-1)
wq = dequantize_int8_channel(qw, scales)
print("per-channel INT8 SNR:", quantize_error(w, wq, metric="snr"))

docs.title: 4. INT4 AWQ (activation-aware)
docs.text:
act_scales = Tensor.randn((w.shape[1],))           # per-input-channel act scale
qw, scales = awq_quantize(w, act_scales, group_size=64)
# (decode path: per-group dequant then matmul — see QuantizedLinear)

docs.title: 5. Quantize the whole model for serving
docs.text:
cfg = QuantizedModelConfig(
    quant_mode=QuantMode.INT4_SYM,
    skip_layers=["lm_head", "embedding.weight"],   # keep embeddings FP32
)
quantized = quantize_model_weights(params, cfg)
print("INT4 size MB:", estimate_model_size_mb(quantized))

docs.title: 6. Round-trip (quantize → dequantize → compare)
docs.text:
restored = dequantize_weights(quantized)
max_err = max(
    np.abs(restored[k].astype(np.float32) - params[k].astype(np.float32)).max()
    for k in ["layers.0.attn.q_proj.weight"]
)
print("max abs error:", max_err)

docs.title: 7. Serve with sneppx-serve
docs.text:
The quantized weights can be saved and loaded by the FastAPI server:

import json, numpy as np
# Save quantized weights as a .npz or safetensors; write a config.
np.savez("/tmp/q_model.npz", **{k: (v.weight.data if hasattr(v, "weight") else v)
                                for k, v in quantized.items()})
cfg_out = {"quant_mode": QuantMode.INT4_SYM, "skip_layers": ["lm_head"]}
json.dump(cfg_out, open("/tmp/q_config.json", "w"))
print("saved /tmp/q_model.npz + /tmp/q_config.json")

Then from the shell:

sneppx-serve --port 8000 --host 127.0.0.1 `
    --auth-mode api-key --api-keys "dev-key" `
    --model-config /tmp/q_config.json --checkpoint /tmp/q_model.npz `
    --disable-output-verify

curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/generate \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer dev-key" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"prompt":"hi","max_new_tokens":8,"do_sample":false}'

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• QuantizedLinear.from_float is the fastest drop-in replacement for a single Linear layer.
  • Whole-model quantization via quantize_model_weights skips embeddings by default — never quantize the LM head if you want stable logits.
  • quantize_error(metric="snr") gives a single scalar for quality; aim for SNR > 20 dB for INT4.
  • sneppx-serve applies the S4/S5 firewall and prompt/output filters by default — pass --disable-* only in trusted environments.

docs.title: Tutorial — Security Scanning
docs.text: Notebook: security_scanning.ipynb (download)

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text: Run the sneppx-analyze static vulnerability scanner on SNEPPX's own C source, inspect the report, and exercise the S0 post-quantum crypto bindings (Dilithium signing, Kyber KEM) from Python.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
# sneppx-analyze is a globally installed tool (sneppx-toolkit[all]):
python -m pip install "sneppx-toolkit[all]"

import json
from SneppX_ALG import Ed25519, Dilithium, KyberKEM, sha256, SecureAllocator
HAS_C = __import__("SneppX_ALG")._HAS_C_BACKEND

docs.title: 1. Scan source with sneppx-analyze
docs.text:
import subprocess

result = subprocess.run(
    ["sneppx-analyze", "scan", "algorithms/hss/core/",
     "--format", "c,h", "--json"],
    capture_output=True, text=True,
)
report = json.loads(result.stdout) if result.stdout else {"findings": []}
print("findings:", len(report.get("findings", [])))
for f in report.get("findings", [])[:5]:
    print(f"  [{f['severity']}] {f['rule']} @ {f['file']}:{f['line']}")

Flags: --format c,h,cu,cpp, --fail-on <info|low|medium|high|critical>, --sarif report.sarif (GitHub-Code-scanning import), --output out.json.

The scanner is static only — it never executes the analyzed code, so it is safe on untrusted sources.

docs.title: 2. Dilithium post-quantum signing (S0)
docs.text:
if HAS_C:
    msg = b"SNEPPX-Algo release v1.2.0"
    dil = Dilithium(level=3)          # FIPS 204 ML-DSA-87
    sig = dil.sign(msg)
    assert dil.verify(msg, sig), "signature invalid"
    print("Dilithium-3 OK, sig len:", len(sig))
else:
    print("C backend required for S0 crypto (build neural_security_c)")

docs.title: 3. Kyber key encapsulation (S0)
docs.text:
if HAS_C:
    kem  = KyberKEM(k=768)            # ML-KEM-768
    ct, sk = kem.encapsulate()
    ss = kem.decapsulate(ct)
    assert ss == sk, "KEM mismatch"
    print("Kyber-768 KEM OK")

docs.title: 4. Hash + secure memory attestation
docs.text:
digest = sha256(b"model-weights.bin")
print("sha256:", digest.hex())

if HAS_C:
    buf = SecureAllocator(8192).alloc()   # guard pages + mlock
    StackCanary().install()
leaks = MemoryLeakDetector().scan()
print("leaks:", leaks)

docs.title: 5. S7 signed-update attestation (CLI)
docs.text:
sneppx-analyze verify model.sneppx --expected-signer "release@snepx"

Verifies the Ed25519 manifest signature embedded by CheckpointWriter.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• sneppx-analyze covers buffer overflows, NULL derefs, integer overflows, uninitialized reads, and crypto-misuse patterns.
  • S0 crypto (Dilithium/Kyber) requires the compiled neural_security_c target.
  • S1 memory hardening (SecureAllocator, guard pages) is always on for the C path; the Python API raises if the backend is missing.
  • Never commit secrets — the scanner flags SNEPPX_secure_free violations (buffers not wiped before free).
